findings.title: Single-game artwork operations check IsLibraryOperationBlocking only at the click, never claim it, so a bulk operation can start and corrupt freshly-loaded entries mid-flight
findings.why_it_matters: A user can click Restore Backup or pick artwork from the grid picker on one row, then click Refresh, Fix Library, Restore Changes or Revert Defaults before the first click's file I/O completes; the second operation replaces the whole game list with newly-built objects, and when the first operation resumes it silently writes its now-stale result onto whichever freshly-loaded entries share that image path instead of being rejected or serialized.
findings.what_is_wrong: IsLibraryOperationBlocking (PrimaryWidget.xaml.cs:191-201) was checked by RestoreBackup_Click (:1857) and GridImage_Click's write path before starting their own single-game async flow, but neither flow ever set isLibraryOperationRunning, so the check only guarded against a bulk operation already running at click time. TryBeginLibraryOperation (:207-220), the guard RefreshButton_Click and ConfirmAndRunAsync's callers already hold for the duration of their own operations, had no awareness of an in-flight single-game write, so it could succeed and let LoadGameEntriesAsync clear and rebuild GameEntries (:359, :695-701) with brand-new GameEntry instances while RestoreBackupCoreAsync's or ReplaceImageCoreAsync's own await was still pending.
evidence: SteamGridDB.Xbox/PrimaryWidget.xaml.cs:191-201 (IsLibraryOperationBlocking - check only, never claims the flag)
SteamGridDB.Xbox/PrimaryWidget.xaml.cs:207-229 (TryBeginLibraryOperation/EndLibraryOperation - the existing guard, unaware of in-flight single-game operations)
findings.leverage_impact: None - this is a missing claim on an already-existing gate, not a Module boundary; the fix reuses TryBeginLibraryOperation/EndLibraryOperation exactly as three other call sites already do.
findings.locality_impact: Fully contained inside PrimaryWidget.xaml.cs; the fix mirrors the idiom that already closed F-001 and F-005 through F-009 in this same file.
findings.why_weakens_submission: Reachable from ordinary UI interaction with no special timing skill required (start a per-game write, then click any header button before it finishes) and silently corrupts user-visible tile state (image, filename, or the backup flag controlling the Restore Backup button's own visibility) with no error surfaced - the same class of harm F-005 through F-009 were rated Serious deduction for, in the same file, discovered from a direction nine prior session-guard sweeps had not checked: per-game-operation versus bulk-operation, rather than per-game-operation versus a second per-game operation.
findings.minimal_correction_path: Extend the guard's claim to the two call sites that actually start an unguarded single-game write reachable from a single click: wrap GridImage_Click's DownloadAndReplaceImageAsync call and RestoreBackup_Click's RestoreBackupAsync call in TryBeginLibraryOperation()/EndLibraryOperation(), the same guard RefreshButton_Click and ConfirmAndRunAsync's callers already hold for their own duration. Do not add the guard inside the shared ReplaceImageCoreAsync/DownloadAndReplaceImageCoreAsync helpers themselves - they are also reached from FixLibraryAsync's bulk loop, which already holds the same non-reentrant guard via ConfirmAndRunAsync, and a second acquire there would reject the bulk operation's own per-game writes.

findings.title: ReplaceImageCoreAsync, RestoreAllChangesAsync and RestoreBackupCoreAsync duplicate the same UI-thread entry-update loop three times

findings.what_is_wrong: ReplaceImageCoreAsync (PrimaryWidget.xaml.cs:1154-1192), RestoreAllChangesAsync's per-entry block (:1067-1135) and RestoreBackupCoreAsync (:1900-1976) each independently dispatch to the UI thread via OnUiThreadAsync and foreach over EntriesSharingImage(game), writing entry.Image and entry.ImageFileName in all three, entry.HasBackup in two of three, and StatusText.Text conditionally in two of three, with no shared helper and no comment distinguishing the field-list differences from oversight.
findings.leverage_impact: Callers currently need to independently verify each of the three copies stays correct; a shared helper would let one Interface carry the invariant.
findings.locality_impact: Change is fully contained inside PrimaryWidget.xaml.cs.
findings.why_weakens_submission: A leaf-duplication pattern already fixed twice in this same file at smaller scope (F-002's animation duplication, F-003's confirmation-dialog duplication) recurring a third time in the entry-update shape reduces confidence the codebase's own established idiom of collapsing on the third instance is being applied consistently.
findings.minimal_correction_path: Extract a private UpdateSharedEntriesAsync(GameEntry game, string imageFileName, BitmapImage image, bool? hasBackup, string statusText) helper (or equivalent) that the three call sites invoke, passing null for the two optional fields where the current behavior omits them; delete the three independent OnUiThreadAsync/foreach blocks.

findings.title: StoreNameLookup's GOG and Epic name caches perform unsynchronized check-then-populate writes, unlike the file's own Ubisoft cache three lines below
findings.why_it_matters: The type's own doc comment says every cache here is shared across the whole process and lives for as long as the widget does, but only one of the three caches (Ubisoft, via AsyncLazyCache<T>) actually protects that shared state from a concurrent check-then-populate race; a future caller that reaches GetOrFetchGogNameAsync or GetOrFetchEpicNameAsync from more than one place at once - or a future fix to Finding F-011's currently-sequential per-entry loop - would silently inherit an unsynchronized Dictionary write with no compiler or test signal.
findings.what_is_wrong: gogNameCache and epicNameCache (StoreNameLookup.cs:29-30) are plain Dictionary<string,string> instances read and written by GetOrFetchGogNameAsync (:89-104) and GetOrFetchEpicNameAsync (:203-222) with a bare check-then-populate (TryGetValue, then an unguarded index-set after an await) and no lock. ubisoftGameListCache (:40-42), three lines below, solves the identical shape - a value loaded once and shared for the process's lifetime - through AsyncLazyCache<T>, which takes a SemaphoreSlim gate specifically so a concurrent caller cannot observe or write a half-populated value. The file implements the same pattern three times with two different concurrency guarantees and no comment explaining why GOG/Epic are exempt from the protection Ubisoft has.
evidence: SteamGridDB.Xbox/Services/Stores/StoreNameLookup.cs:40-42 (ubisoftGameListCache - same shape, properly gated via AsyncLazyCache<T>)
SteamGridDB.Xbox/Services/AsyncLazyCache.cs:19-60 (the existing gated-cache primitive already available to reuse)
findings.leverage_impact: A caller of GetOrFetchGogNameAsync/GetOrFetchEpicNameAsync today gets no guarantee about concurrent-access safety from the Interface alone - it has to read the implementation to learn it is currently safe only because its sole caller (LoadGameEntriesAsync) happens to await sequentially.
findings.locality_impact: Fully contained inside StoreNameLookup.cs; the fix reuses the file's own existing AsyncLazyCache<T>-based gate idiom rather than inventing a new one.
findings.why_weakens_submission: Not currently reachable as a live race (LoadGameEntriesAsync's only caller awaits each entry in strict sequence, per Finding F-011's own evidence), so this is latent rather than a Serious deduction - but it is a real structural inconsistency: the same file solves the identical problem two different ways with no stated reason, which is exactly the kind of drift-inviting pattern the codebase's own doc comments elsewhere go out of their way to prevent (see AppliedArtworkStore.cs's explicit comment on why GetAsync and UpdateAsync share one gate).
findings.minimal_correction_path: Replace gogNameCache/epicNameCache's raw Dictionary fields with a per-key gated cache, or - smaller - wrap the existing check-then-populate body of GetOrFetchGogNameAsync/GetOrFetchEpicNameAsync in the same SemaphoreSlim gate field ubisoftGameListCache already uses, matching AppliedArtworkStore's own pattern of one shared gate serializing multiple methods against the same Dictionary.

findings.title: GamePlatformHelper's Xbox-folder-name and SteamGridDB-API-string mappings are two independent switch statements over GamePlatform with no shared source of truth
findings.why_it_matters: Adding a ninth platform, or renaming an existing one, requires remembering to update both switch statements; nothing fails to compile if one is forgotten, since both already have a default case that silently returns Unknown or null rather than erroring.
findings.what_is_wrong: GamePlatformHelper.FromXboxDirectory (GamePlatform.cs:22-46) maps an Xbox ThirdPartyLibraries folder name to GamePlatform; GamePlatformHelper.GamePlatformToSGDBApiString (GamePlatform.cs:48-67) maps GamePlatform back to SteamGridDB's own platform strings. Both switch over the same enum with the same six platform cases (Steam, GOG, Epic, Ubisoft, BattleNet, EA) independently authored, with no shared table and no exhaustiveness check tying them together.
findings.leverage_impact: Each new platform pays this asserted-twice tax; small at 6 cases, would compound at 15+.
findings.why_weakens_submission: Minor, but is exactly the shape a domain-modeling 10 would not have: the enum's own home module holds two independent interpretations of itself with no compiler-enforced link.
findings.minimal_correction_path: Fold both mappings into one table (a single static Dictionary<GamePlatform,(string XboxFolder,string SgdbId)> or a per-case record list) that both directions read from, so a missing platform in one direction becomes a missing table row rather than a second, independently-authored switch.

findings.why_it_matters: On a library with many unmatched games, the fully-sequential per-entry network chain adds latency that scales linearly with library size, all before the widget shows anything.

findings.locality_impact: Would be contained to PrimaryWidget.xaml.cs and StoreNameLookup.cs's cache-locking prerequisite (F-015), if unblocked.

builder_notes.pattern: A mutual-exclusion guard's real coverage is defined by which call sites hold it, not by its own doc comment or by the check-only callers that read it.
builder_notes.how_to_recognize: Grep every caller of a boolean 'IsXBlocking()'-style check function; for each one, confirm it also calls the paired 'TryBeginX()/EndX()' claim around its own work, not just the read-only check before starting.
builder_notes.smallest_coding_rule: A guard-check function whose name is a present-participle predicate ('...Blocking', '...Running', '...Busy') is a signal to verify a matching Begin/End pair exists at every caller that performs the guarded work, not only the callers that look 'library-wide' at a glance.
builder_notes.stack_example: C#: `if (IsBusy) return;` without a paired `IsBusy = true; try { ... } finally { IsBusy = false; }` around the actual work is a check without a claim - exactly what let F-014 (and originally F-005 through F-009) through several prior review passes.

builder_notes.pattern: The same small primitive (a gated lazy cache) gets reinvented per-field instead of reused, and only the newest field gets the lock.
builder_notes.how_to_recognize: Grep for `Dictionary<...>` fields marked `static` or otherwise process-lifetime, each paired with a `TryGetValue`-then-conditional-write method nearby. If a sibling field in the same file uses a proper gate (SemaphoreSlim, lock, or a shared cache type) and this one doesn't, that's the tell.
builder_notes.smallest_coding_rule: When a file already has one correctly-locked cache, a second cache added later should reuse the same gate or cache type, not hand-roll its own check-then-populate.
builder_notes.stack_example: C#: this codebase's own AsyncLazyCache<T> (Services/AsyncLazyCache.cs) already solves this; StoreNameLookup's Ubisoft cache uses it, its GOG/Epic caches (added earlier) don't.

builder_notes.pattern: A near-identical block appearing a third time in one file is this codebase's own established threshold for 'extract it' - it collapsed F-002 at 4 copies and F-003 at 3.
builder_notes.how_to_recognize: Two similar-looking blocks might be coincidence; a third, especially one that's already drifted in one field, means the shared shape needs one owner.
builder_notes.smallest_coding_rule: On finding a third near-identical block, extract before writing a fourth - not after.
builder_notes.stack_example: n/a - general pattern, already demonstrated twice in this same file's history (F-002, F-003); F-013 is a not-yet-collapsed third instance of the same shape.

builder_notes.how_to_recognize: n/a - this entry is a non-blocking self-audit (Q9), not a code pattern.
builder_notes.stack_example: Three claims this loop's critic is least confident about: (1) credibility at 9.5 rather than 9.0 - F-015 is Noticeable, not Cosmetic, and a stricter reading could cap any Noticeable-severity residual at 9.0; 9.5 was judged defensible because F-015 is genuinely local and subtractive-fixable, matching the 9-anchor's own language, but this is a judgment call rather than a bright line. (2) state_management held at 7.0 despite fixing F-014 this loop - this follows the project's own established convention (score reflects pre-fix source; credit lands next loop against this loop's commit sha) rather than crediting the fix immediately, which a reviewer could reasonably expect same-loop credit for. (3) F-015's severity at Noticeable rather than Serious - judged latent (no reachable concurrent caller found) rather than live, based on LoadGameEntriesAsync's single sequential per-entry loop being StoreNameLookup's sole caller; if some other code path reaches it concurrently that this loop's bounded read did not find, the severity should be higher.

narrative: Place, not win, yet. The codebase has real depth in its artwork pipeline and increasingly disciplined ownership in PrimaryWidget.xaml.cs, but this loop independently re-derived and closed the sixth-and-latest instance of a defect class (reentrancy gaps between per-game and library-wide operations) that nine prior loops of dedicated sweeps had not fully closed - runtime ownership is more trustworthy after this loop's fix than before it, but a well-reviewed guard's own doc comment being incomplete for this long is a caution against declaring the class closed. Concurrency remains trustworthy for what actually runs today (nothing executes off the UI thread), though this loop surfaced a latent inconsistency (F-015) worth closing before any future change makes cache access concurrent. Simplification helped this loop: the fix reused an existing primitive rather than inventing a new guard type. Tests do not, and structurally cannot, reduce regression risk on PrimaryWidget.xaml.cs itself - every finding in this file, including this loop's, was found and verified by direct reading and unchanged build/test evidence, not by a failing test turning green.
